questions.q: What is OLTP storage optimized for?
options: Fast single-row reads and writes, like a vendor's live booking system
Aggregating across millions of rows at once
Cheap, durable storage of raw files with no fast query pattern
Real-time alerting on streaming data
questions.explain: This is a row-oriented shape, distinct from OLAP's column-oriented aggregation strength.

questions.q: What is the one question that actually decides between OLTP, OLAP, and object storage?
options: How is the data actually going to be read?
Which storage option is cheapest per gigabyte?
Which storage option is easiest to set up?
Which programming language will query it?
questions.explain: A single-row update pattern favors OLTP; an aggregation-across-millions-of-rows pattern favors OLAP; a durable-raw-file pattern favors object storage.

questions.q: Why does "average fare across 200,000 trips" favor OLAP over OLTP?
options: It only needs to read a single FareAmount column across every row, which is exactly what column-oriented storage is efficient at, rather than reading whole rows one at a time
OLTP systems are physically incapable of running aggregation queries
OLAP is always faster than OLTP for every kind of query
This scenario actually favors OLTP, not OLAP
questions.explain: Columnar scan efficiency is exactly what OLAP storage is built for.

questions.q: How does the medallion architecture (Databricks & Delta Lake) relate to this lesson's storage choices?
options: It formalizes the idea of combining storage shapes — raw object storage (bronze) feeds cleaned object storage (silver) feeds an OLAP-shaped serving layer (gold)
The medallion architecture only ever uses OLTP storage
It replaces the need to choose between OLTP, OLAP, and object storage
It's unrelated to storage shape and only concerns compute
questions.explain: Real systems combine all three storage shapes rather than forcing one to do every job.

questions.q: Why does forcing one storage shape to do every job (e.g., OLTP for analytics) work badly?
options: Each part of a real platform has a different read pattern, and a storage shape optimized for one pattern performs poorly on a fundamentally different one
It actually works fine in every case, and using one storage type is always simpler
OLTP and OLAP are technically identical under the hood
This only matters for systems processing more than a petabyte of data
questions.explain: This is why the real question is "which one, for which part," not "which one for the whole platform."
